• Scientific name: Thor amboinensis
  • Other names: Sexy anemone shrimp, Anemone shrimp, Squat shrimp, Humpback shrimp, High-tailed shrimp, Pikmin shrimp, Dancing shrimp
  • Minimum tank size: 20 litres
  • Keeping: easy; breeding: difficult
  • Water type: SG 1.023–1.025
  • Optimal KH: 7–12
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: carnivore
  • Temperament: peaceful
  • Colour: orange with a number of large white spots outlined in blue

Thor amboinensis is a circumtropical symbiotic species found on coral reefs in all tropical oceans, from the Red Sea through the Indo-Pacific, Caribbean and Atlantic, ending at the Canary Islands off the coast of Africa.

  • Western Atlantic: Bahamas, southern Florida, Caribbean Sea, Brazil.
  • Eastern Atlantic: Madeira, Canary Islands, Cape Verde Islands.
  • Indo-West Pacific: Kenya, Madagascar, Bay of Bengal, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Japan, Taiwan, Philippines, Indonesia, Palau Islands, Caroline Islands, Marshall Islands, Australia.
  • Eastern Pacific: Costa Rica (Cocos Island), Panama (Pearl Islands), Ecuador, Chile (Easter Island).

The 'Sexy' Shrimp lives on coral reefs at depths of at least 2 to 25 m, usually within the tentacles of various sea anemones. Occasionally it is found free-living in dead corals, small cracks in rocks and in biogenic gravels.

Thor amboinensis has been recorded in association with at least 12 different genera of sea anemones, such as Telmatactis cricoides, Stichodactyla spp., Cryptodendrum adhaesivum, Macrodactyla doreensis, Phymanthus sp., Heteractis spp., Actinodendron plumosum, Anemonia sulcata, Zoanthus sp., Lebrunia danae and Entacmaea quadricolor.

Shrimp that associate with habitat providers ('hosts') may obtain physical shelter from predation, camouflage, stability, range expansion or advantageous positioning. In return, they clean the anemones. Most often they consume planktonic organisms caught by the anemone's tentacles. Contact between the shrimp and the tentacles does not trigger the anemone's feeding reaction; the tentacles do not cling to the shrimp and the shrimp showed no signs of being stung.

During the day the shrimp can be found on the substrate near the tentacles, on the column of the anemone and occasionally on the tentacles and the oral disk. At night, when the anemone contracts its tentacles, the shrimp usually move either to the column or away from the anemone.

Thor amboinensis has been observed sharing the same host with other shrimps and even the spider crab Mithrax sp. Groups usually contain adults and much smaller individuals. The shrimp are attracted to their host anemone mainly by chemical signals.
Minimum tank size: 20 litres. A species tank is ideal, and keeping a group requires more space. Their small size makes them perfect for limited space such as nano reef tanks.

Keeping Sexy shrimp is not complicated because they have no special water quality requirements; they should be kept under conditions suitable for any typical reef aquarium inhabitant.

Tank décor should include plenty of structures where the shrimp can hide, especially when they are young.

They need careful acclimation, as all invertebrates do. Do it very slowly; 2–3 hours is generally good enough. They do not like swings in salinity.

• Salinity: specific gravity 1.023–1.025.
  • Temperature: about 22–28°C, with 24–27°C optimal.
  • pH: 8.1–8.4.
  • Alkalinity: 7–12 dKH, although it often goes a little higher or lower.
  • Calcium: 400–450 ppm is optimal, but it can be a bit lower or higher.
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm.
  • Iodine is believed by many to be important for moulting; use an iodine additive according to the manufacturer's instructions.
Basic tank equipment: filter, air pump, heater, substrate, live rock, sea salt, test kits and a hydrometer or salinity refractometer for measuring seawater.

Feeding is easy. The 'Sexy' Shrimp is a carnivore and accepts a wide range of fish, shrimp or anemone foods. No direct feeding is necessary where there are anemones or corals, as they can feed off coral slime and the organisms trapped in it.

If the tank has no anemones, they need food. They are too often viewed as simple scavengers expected to survive on leftovers from feeding community fish. This is problematic: leftover food means the tank is being overfed, and the solution is to feed less; and they should not be treated just as janitors.

They do best on sinking food. Any pellet, flake or gel food that provides animal-based nutrition will work. Meaty food with higher fat content can accelerate breeding, but risks water quality problems. Many good frozen foods also sink and make an excellent diet, especially when trying to breed them.

The common name comes from its unusual dance: it holds its abdomen up in the air and waves it up and down, almost all the time. The abdomen and tail arch upward towards the head.

They are completely peaceful and usually do not bother anybody in the tank. They are also very social and tend to gather in large groups, which may reflect their small size and limited defensive ability. They often share a hiding place, and in a group they feel more relaxed and confident, although they lack social structure.

They can move very quickly, covering short distances of 15–20 cm in the blink of an eye. The species is usually associated with corals and anemones, but in aquariums it can also live without any anemones.

Reef safety: in most cases there are no problems in reef tanks. However, some individuals may go into 'rogue mode' and start picking at corals; some aquarists report that they eat SPS frags and destroy polyps. Watch them closely at the beginning.

Tankmates: the ideal is a species tank, but they can be kept with other fish chosen with care. Aggressive eaters should be avoided. Large predators such as triggerfish, wrasses, hawkfish and angelfish are unsuitable, and so are clownfish, which do not tolerate anyone in their anemone. They get along well with their own kind, so a group is not a problem but needs more space. Boxer crabs, snails (cerith, bumble bee, conch, nassarius, etc.), porcelain crabs, emerald crabs, cleaner shrimp (spotted anemone shrimp, peppermint shrimp, red fire shrimp, skunk cleaner shrimp, red-white cleaner shrimp), saron shrimp and bumble bee shrimp usually do not bother them. Porcelain anemone crabs, which also need anemones, should not be a problem as they do not compete for them.

• The larger Sexy Shrimp are females; males are smaller (usually only up to 1.5 cm).
  • In the absolute majority of cases, in females the white stripe across the back is broken. Males do not have a broken stripe; it looks like a single dot or stripe.
  • Because females carry eggs, their underside (abdomen) is wider and curves down to protect the eggs. Males are thinner.

Breeding is tricky and difficult. The few existing larval descriptions and the lack of knowledge of larval morphology and development of Thor species are bottlenecks for captive production. Few aquarists can do it systematically and successfully.

  • Thor amboinensis is a protandric hermaphrodite: it first matures as a male and changes to female later in life, usually once it reaches 15–18 mm.
  • Each spawn can produce several hundred eggs (100–300); clutch size increases approximately exponentially with female size.
  • Larvae typically hatch within 14–20 days of fertilization. As the larvae develop, the eggs progress from yellow towards transparency.
  • Embryos hatch as planktonic larvae called zoeae. The larva goes through 8 stages and one decapodid before settling.
  • Larval duration is 26–28 days; complete transformation can take another 10–12 days. Under laboratory conditions the moult to decapodid occurred 28 days after hatching.

Rearing larvae

  • Water parameters are the same.
  • Use no substrate, rocks or decorations – just a bare bottom with heater and airstone. The flow should constantly move the larvae but not fast.
  • Do not use sea anemones in rearing setups; in laboratory conditions the anemone consumed larvae.
  • Larval food quality and quantity and stocking density are important factors for larval survival.
  • Separate the larvae from the main tank. Ideally use cylindrico-conical recirculation tanks, whose shape gives the best circulation and prevents larvae touching the glass; if they touch the wall they cannot detach and die.
  • Stock at about 40 larvae in 10-litre tanks.
  • Do 30–50% water changes twice a day (morning and night).
  • Diet is extremely important: feed freshly hatched baby brine shrimp (about 10,000 nauplii per litre) twice a day or they die. They only eat the yolk sac of the brine shrimp, which lasts only 12 hours.

Zoea sizes: first 1.99–2.30 mm; second 2.16–2.50 mm; third 2.52–2.74 mm; fourth 2.98–3.38 mm; fifth 3.35–3.85 mm; sixth 3.62–3.85 mm; seventh 4.08–4.38 mm; eighth 4.31–4.61 mm; decapodid 4.41–4.52 mm.

The common name refers to its usually raised tail and the curious way it sways its abdomen back and forth when walking. This behaviour and its colours contribute to its popularity in the ornamental trade. Adults are usually less than 2 cm; females are bigger than males. The shrimp have short-stalked eyes protruding from the carapace, and a well-developed rostrum that does not reach beyond the eyes or expand ventrally. The colouring is distinctive orange with large white spots outlined in blue. In a proper aquarium with optimum conditions they can grow, reproduce and live up to 3 years.
